recommendations.title: Show HN: Benchmarks of continual learning model trained for a month on a laptop
recommendations.summary:
A month ago, I shared mini-AGI, an experiment in training a byte-level, continually learning language model from scratch on a single 8 GB laptop GPU (an RTX 3070). To recap the setup briefly: it completely decouples model size from VRAM by paging experts to and from an NVMe drive (currently 397 experts / 1.26B total parameters on disk, with only 32 resident / ~109M active in 5.1 GB of VRAM). It trains on a single stream at batch 1, with the attention/embedding trunk learning rate dampened to 0.1x to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.

The training is still going and went only through ~35% of the training corpus selected at the beginning of the run (about 8GB in total). Here is the current status:

1. enwik9 (First 10^9 bytes of English Wikipedia):

    Model               Params   Data Read       Cost     enwik9 (bits/byte) ↓

    Llama-3.2-1B        1.23B    36 TB (9T tok)  ~$900k   0.68
    Chinchilla 1B       1.00B    5.6 TB          ~$68k    0.90
    GPT-2 XL            1.56B    40 GB           ~$43k    1.07
    GPT-2 Large         0.77B    40 GB           ~$21k    1.12
    mini-AGI (online)   1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.14
    GPT-2 Medium        0.35B    40 GB           ~$10k    1.17
    mini-AGI (dynamic)  1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.23
    mini-AGI (frozen)   1.26B    2.8 GB          ~$56     1.29
    GPT-2 Small         0.12B    40 GB           ~$3k     1.33
2. PG19 (100 Project Gutenberg books, 41 MB test split):

    Model               Params   Trained On        Cost    PG19 (bits/byte) ↓

    MambaByte-972M       0.97B   75 GB (PG19)      ~$4k    0.883
    MegaByte-1B          1.02B   80 GB (PG19)      ~$1.6k  1.000
    Transformer-320M     0.32B   80 GB (PG19)      ~$1.6k  1.057
    mini-AGI (online)    1.26B   2.8 GB (0 PG19)   ~$56    1.447
    mini-AGI (frozen)    1.26B   2.8 GB (0 PG19)   ~$56    1.995

    The published models were trained on PG19's own training books, 75 to 80 GB of them, and are scored on more books like those. mini-AGI has never been trained on PG19 and has read no Victorian novels, so for it these books are completely out of its domain.
There are more details in the repository. The most important part is a difference between "frozen" and "online" attempts where we allow the model to specialize on the task as it goes through the evaluation dataset. Clearly showcasing the power of continual learning regime simply unavailable for any other typical LLM.

Full methodology, and replication code is in the repo: https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI

Intermediate weights snapshot on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/Volotat/mini-AGI-undertrained

recommendations.title: Show HN: Claude Code(and others) embedded in your app
recommendations.summary:
I started this project in 2024 when I got fascinated with LLMs, and what I did was a coding agent (CLI -> interactive -> GUI). I also added an integration with Vite for having it embedded inside my apps(mostly games). Few months ago I pivoted it to become a low profile AI provider wrapper library (think jQuery for LLM usage), because I realized there is no point to have custom coding agent.

Recently I did yet another pivot, and now it is a solution that allows you to embed Claude Code inside of your app, and use it directly from there for 1. development, 2. every day ops and automate the tasks in the app

In theory all you need to try it is this command: `npx genaicode embed`, I wonder if anyone would like to give it a try, and let me know how it worked!

recommendations.title: Ask HN: Kimi Code hit its 5-hour limit after $1.37 of API usage
recommendations.summary:
I paid $19 for Kimi Code to test K3.1 Pro Standard (not Highspeed) using the official CLI v2.3.1.

I ran two tasks on small repositories:

1. Recommend movies based on an existing movie database. 2. Analyze a website's codebase.

Neither task completed. The entire 5-hour quota was exhausted within minutes.

I analyzed the actual session logs, including background agents:

- Fresh input: 368,203 tokens - Cached input: 1,183,744 tokens - Output: 39,324 tokens - Total: 1.59M tokens

At Kimi's published API rates, that's just $1.37 worth of usage before hitting the 5-hour limit which is easily less than 5% of what Claude Code offers at $20 subscription.

The logs show: "429 You've reached your 5-hour usage limit."

For comparison, Claude Code on a $20 subscription processed roughly 381M tokens over 4-5 hours using Opus 5.5 xhigh, mostly cached input. That's not a controlled benchmark, but the difference in usable capacity is staggering.

Both Kimi tasks failed without delivering results. I have video evidence and detailed logs, but won't publish private repository data.

Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hSr-DLn88AM

Is this a quota-accounting bug, or are Kimi's $19 subscription limits intentionally this restrictive?

Disclosure: I also develop a competing coding agent. These tests used Kimi's official CLI.

links.title: Is AI just another get rich quick scheme?
links.summary:
You too can get rich quick in real estate --- details in this book; only $49.95.

If there really was a sure fire way to get rich quick, why sell books to the public? Why not keep it to yourself and apply it to make money?

The same applies to AI. If it was really all that, they wouldn't be selling tokens to the public. They would be forming corporate partnerships, building products and conquering markets --- starting with the financial markets.

Those who can --- do. Those who can't --- sell books and "tokens".

links.author: utku1337

links.title: Show HN: A client-side adaptive cognitive test measuring micro-hesitations
links.summary:
Hi HN! I’m not a software engineer by trade. My background is in behavioral science and human-computer interaction, but I wanted to solve a specific problem I found when applying for jobs which is the logical test. They are booooring, easy to cheat on if you really want to and provides very limited information about people. I built this prototype from scratch sing AI to bring my idea to life. So now I've been working on this side project for a Cognitive Adaption Engine (CAT/KAT in swedish) for about three weeks. Many pre-employment screening tests i've done use a static item bank and are very liberal with the time allowed on each question, making it easy for Vision LLMs or bots to beat. I wanted to see if I could build a fast, client-side engine (JS/SVG) that combats this problem by measuring certain biometric cognitive signatures like "switch cost" (how long it takes for your brain to re-adjust when logical rules change) and "post error-slowing". To go beyond the simple grading of correct/incorrect, this test dynamically gives you waves of patterns/challenges through a local item bank based on your millisecond response times. If you use an LLM, the constant latencies gets punished with a lower score. If they use a script, the complete lack of natural human variance will be picked up on. I am currently trying to calibrate a baseline and need high-aptitude users to stress-test it and to provide more data. It also makes it very fast to complete.

Everything runs 100% locally in your browser and since I did use AI, I would love your feedback on how the architecture holds up and the technical approach to anti-cheating or anything that comes to mind on this topic.

(Optional) When you finish the test, you can press Ctrl + Shift + X on the results page which unlocks a hidden admin console. There you can see more info on your performance and even download a HR-pdf that translate your data into three tailored interview questions. Unfortunately the admin page is in Swedish, but I believe you will get the idea.
